title: Responsibility depends on whether harm was foreseeable, not on intent or impact
dek: Shouting insults at someone is your responsibility; if a harmless compliment destroys the listener, that's mostly their past experiences at play—not something to wholly pin on the speaker.
why: No new data or research models—just two people parsing concepts around intent versus impact and victim mentality through their own experiences. Think of it as a deep conversation rather than a how-to list.
who: Anyone trying to sort out whether they should blame themselves in personal conflicts, and parents raising children with atypical emotional or autonomy needs.
skip: 44:25-52:35, on likability and workplace support-group feedback, is lower density and can be skipped.

points.h: Self-responsibility and "impact over intent" contradict each other
points.body: Shawni points out that workplace interpersonal skills training teaches "self-responsibility"—you're only responsible for what you say, not how the other person receives it—which directly conflicts with the popular "impact matters more than intent": the former says you can't control the other's reaction, the latter says the other's reaction is all that counts. Both believe no one sits at one extreme of the spectrum, but which way you lean depends on the specific situation.

points.h: Whether you could foresee harm is the true line for responsibility
points.body: Spencer gives examples: shouting an insult at someone has foreseeable consequences, so the speaker bears full responsibility; but saying "I like your hairstyle," which seems harmless, might devastate someone with hidden past experiences—that's more "their issue." Shawni adds that cultural pressure to never "assume what someone else has experienced" actually puts everyone on eggshells—you never know if an innocuous remark will hit a buried wound.

points.h: With no arbiter, accusations and defenses just become he-said-she-said
points.body: Shawni points to an unsolvable deadlock: if one person says "what you said made me think I'd misremembered, so you're gaslighting me" and the other says "I remember it completely differently," no one can rule on whether gaslighting actually happened. She worries therapy language is slapping pathological labels onto ordinary interpersonal friction, and the person applying the label naturally holds the power to define it.

points.h: A friend's comfort can be reverse gaslighting
points.body: Spencer coins a term, "light gassing": the opposite of gaslighting, when a friend reinforces an already mistaken perception—"he's just a jerk, you did nothing wrong." He says this is usually not malicious; friends just want to be good friends based on what they hear. But it prevents anyone from solving the problem because no one turns it around and asks "so what are you going to do?"

points.h: External locus of control makes everything feel like something being done to you
points.body: Shawni introduces the concept of locus of control: people with external locus feel things "happen to them," while those with internal locus feel they're the captain. She's noticed chronically troubled friends often have stronger external locus—once you think that way, "impact versus intent" naturally tips toward impact because you already see the other person as doing something to you, not as both of you participating in an interaction.

points.h: Victim narrative keeps itself alive with its own evidence
points.body: Using Lena Dunham's book as an example, Shawni describes a slide: from "I was victimized in this one thing" to "my whole life is victimhood." She keeps telling friends what happened to her, they gradually wear out and pull away, and she treats that distance as new proof that "people are hurting me"—self-reinforcing, leaving no room for self-responsibility. Spencer adds that even genuine victims, if they interpret victimhood as "I'm completely helpless," may end up harming themselves.

points.h: Catch more abusers or protect more innocent people?
points.body: Spencer frames the social-media phenomenon of masses labeling someone a gaslighter or narcissist as a false-positive versus false-negative trade-off: do you cast a wide net for abusers and risk hurting some innocents, or stay strict and let real abusers slip through? His solution is precision in language—instead of saying "this person is a narcissist," spell out exactly which diagnostic criteria for narcissistic personality disorder they actually fit, so the label actually communicates something.

points.h: Looks like spoiling a child; actually lifesaving
points.body: Shawni's older daughter has a form of autism recognized in the UK but not widely acknowledged in Canada or the US called PDA (pathological demand avoidance): everyday tasks like brushing teeth or putting on shoes drain her "stress cup," and when it fills up, there's a meltdown. Standard advice is exposure therapy—push her to overcome her fear—which Shawni tried, and it sent her daughter into a week-long shutdown where she couldn't speak or eat. Switching to giving options and using statements rather than questions to remove the sense of demand worked—but to outsiders, it looks exactly like indulging a "spoiled" child.

terms.def: The degree to which you believe you control your own outcomes (internal) versus events happening to you (external).
A friend reinforcing an already mistaken belief instead of helping you see straight—the opposite of gaslighting.
A profile within autism where everyday demands like brushing teeth trigger severe stress; needs high autonomy to function.
Speaking in statements—"the shoes are here"—rather than questions, to remove the felt pressure of being told what to do.
Addressing only the core problem while ignoring context, which can make the other person feel their emotions are dismissed.

quotes.text: So self-responsibility means I'm responsible for the way that I interact with you, the things that I say to a certain degree, but I'm not responsible for the way that you receive that information.
There's no magical adjudicator in the middle of the conversation that says, "Yes, this fits all the criteria for gaslighting."
I actually have a term I call "light gassing" for when someone reinforces your false perceptions, so it's the opposite of gaslighting.

If we are someone with an external locus of control, you're much more likely to perceive things as happening to you and be back in that space where intent versus impact matters more than self-responsibility.
Over time, people got exhausted or tired by the conversation, so they started to pull back. By them pulling back, it's another checkbox for her in this list of things she's been a victim of

Would you rather have it be that more abusers get caught, but then sometimes innocent people get caught up in it and falsely accused, or that fewer abusers get caught, and more are just out there, and nobody knows that they're abusing, but you're protecting innocent people?
